case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. A.W.
key_cases.holding: Reversing termination, the Court set out the four-part best-interests standard for terminating parental rights under N.J.S.A. 30:4C-15(c) and held the Division must prove it by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: A.W. is the source of New Jersey's four-prong best-interests test and its clear-and-convincing burden for terminating parental rights.
key_cases.quote: The child's health and development have been or will be seriously impaired by the parental relationship.

key_cases.holding: The Court reinstated termination, holding a child born drug-addicted whose mother cannot care for her at birth is endangered under prong one and that the four statutory criteria overlap rather than operate discretely.
key_cases.relevance: K.H.O. is the Supreme Court's controlling construction of each prong of N.J.S.A. 30:4C-15.1(a) in termination cases.
key_cases.quote: We hold that a child's health and development are endangered when she is born drug addicted and her mother cannot care for her at birth.

key_cases.case_name: N.J. Division of Child Protection & Permanency v. R.L.M. (In re R.A.J.)
key_cases.holding: The Court held that under N.J.S.A. 30:4C-15.4 a parent may proceed pro se in a termination action, subject to timely and unequivocal invocation and the court's discretion to appoint standby counsel.
key_cases.relevance: R.L.M. governs a parent's choice between appointed counsel and self-representation in a termination trial.
key_cases.quote: The parent's right of self-representation, however, is by no means absolute.

key_cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. R.G.
key_cases.holding: The Court reinstated the trial court's denial of guardianship, holding that incarceration alone, without particularized evidence of its effect on each best-interests prong, cannot support termination.
key_cases.relevance: R.G. controls termination cases involving incarcerated parents and requires prong-by-prong proof rather than reliance on the fact of imprisonment.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the trial court's finding that the Division failed to prove its case by clear and convincing evidence is supported by the trial evidence

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that due process requires at least clear and convincing evidence before a State may terminate parental rights, invalidating New York's fair-preponderance standard.
key_cases.relevance: Santosky fixes the federal constitutional burden of proof that New Jersey's termination standard implements.
key_cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held there is no automatic federal right to appointed counsel in termination proceedings; the Mathews factors are weighed case by case against a presumption that appointed counsel is required only where physical liberty is at stake.
key_cases.relevance: Lassiter is the federal baseline on appointed counsel in termination cases, which New Jersey exceeds by statute and by B.R.
key_cases.quote: It is against this presumption that all the other elements in the due process decision must be measured.

key_cases.case_name: In re the Guardianship of J.C.
key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination and remanded, holding that where termination rests on the child's bond with foster parents rather than current unfitness, the Division must prove by clear and convincing evidence, through a qualified expert who also evaluates the child's relationship with the natural parent, that separation would cause serious and enduring harm.
key_cases.relevance: J.C. is the foundational New Jersey decision on the fourth best-interests prong, setting the bonding and psychological-parent proofs a termination judgment must rest on.
key_cases.quote: DYFS must prove by clear and convincing evidence that separating the child from his or her foster parents would cause serious and enduring emotional or psychological harm.

key_cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. F.M.
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed the termination of a mother's parental rights, holding that substantial and credible evidence supported each of the four best-interests prongs, including that her inability to shield the children from their dangerous father satisfied prongs one and two and that the Division's enumerated services satisfied the reasonable-efforts prong.
key_cases.relevance: F.M. is the Court's most comprehensive modern restatement of the four-prong best-interests test and the deference owed to the family court's termination judgment.
key_cases.quote: Ultimately, a child has a right to live in a stable, nurturing environment and to have the psychological security that his most deeply formed attachments will not be shattered.

key_cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. E.P.
key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination of an unfit mother's parental rights to her emotionally fragile twelve-year-old daughter, holding the Division failed to prove on the fourth prong that severing the child's only enduring bond would not do more harm than good when adoption was a remote prospect.
key_cases.relevance: E.P. limits termination where permanency through adoption is unlikely, and is the Court's fullest treatment of an older, troubled child's own attachments and therapeutic needs in the best-interests analysis.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the family court was clearly mistaken in finding that the Division satisfied the four-prong best-interests-of-the-child test and in terminating Andrea's relationship with her mother.

extended_foster_care_age: Up to age 21, and only on conditions: the Department of Children and Families provides services to an individual between 18 and 21 years of age who meets all three conditions of N.J.S.A. 30:4C-2.3 together — (a) the individual was receiving services from the department on or after the individual's 16th birthday; (b) the individual has not, on or after the individual's 18th birthday, refused or requested that these services be terminated; and (c) the commissioner determines that a continuation of services would be in the individual's best interest and would assist the individual to become an independent and productive adult (law.justia.com/codes/new-jersey/title-30/section-30-4c-2-3/)
